sessions.title: The Success Triangle
sessions.key_problem: Early in a sales career, not yet seeing that lasting success comes from attitude, behavior, and technique combined, and that self-image and belief quietly cap what's achievable.
sessions.light_bulb: Success requires all three legs of the Success Triangle (Attitude, Behavior, Technique) together, and results are capped by self-image and beliefs, so changing outcomes starts with changing what you believe, not just what you do.
sessions.scenario: Early in a sales career, focusing only on scripts and tactics but hitting an invisible ceiling because underlying beliefs and self-image haven't changed.
key_rules: If you manage results, you manage the past. If you manage behavior, you manage the future.
There is a difference between who you "I" and what you "R"
You cannot outperform your own self image
If you want to change what you've always achieved, you must first change what you have always believed

sessions.title: The Buyer-Seller Dynamic
sessions.key_problem: Unknowingly letting the prospect run a defensive buyer process (Express Interest, Act Motivated, Obtain Information, Avoid Commitment, Disappear) in parallel with the sales process, handing over free consulting and losing control before the close.
sessions.light_bulb: Two processes run at once -- the sales process and the buyer's -- and the moment a full Present/Propose goes out without qualifying first, the buyer has everything needed and disappears, so control is lost long before the 'attempt to close' step.
sessions.scenario: Great presentations and proposals keep going nowhere because the prospect was quietly running their own playbook the whole time, and it went unnoticed.
key_rules: All prospects lie, all the time
Prescription without diagnosis is malpractice
Live a straight life in an un-straight world and you're gonna get killed
When you want to know the future, bring it back to the present.

links.mac_deck: /Users/danfaber/Documents/Training/Beautiful AI Decks 2026/Essentials - Sales/02. The Buyer-Seller Dynamic.pptx

sessions.title: Communication Skills
sessions.key_problem: Building rapport the same generic way with every prospect instead of adapting communication style to the buyer's personality, and undercutting credibility by over-answering, over-pitching, or oversharing too soon.
sessions.light_bulb: Real rapport comes from matching and mirroring a prospect's DISC style rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, and oversharing personal info or product knowledge too early ('spilling your candy in the lobby') breaks trust instead of building it.
sessions.scenario: Every call sounds identical, with no clue why some prospects click instantly and others go cold the moment the talking starts.
key_rules: If your competition does it, stop doing it right away.
A prospect who is listening is no prospect at all.
It's more important that the prospect bonds with you than you bond with the prospect.
Don't spill your candy in the lobby.
All prospects lie, all the time. Unless they don't have to.
Product knowledge used at the wrong time can be intimidating.

links.mac_deck: /Users/danfaber/Documents/Training/Beautiful AI Decks 2026/Essentials - Sales/03. Communication Skills.pptx

sessions.title: Initiating Buyer Focused Conversations
sessions.key_problem: Inconsistent prospecting and too few referral asks because it feels greedy or awkward, leaving the new-business pipeline thin and dependent on lower-converting sources.
sessions.light_bulb: Referrals close far more often than cold calls (55% vs 2% in this deck's data), so conviction in your own product plus a deliberate, unapologetic prospecting cadence — not liking the activity — is what fixes a thin pipeline.
sessions.scenario: New-meeting numbers keep falling short, and referral asks keep getting avoided because they feel pushy or greedy.
key_rules: You never have to like prospecting, you just have to do it
A winner has alternatives, a loser puts all their eggs in one basket
Every unsuccessful prospecting call earns compound interest
Effort = Control

sessions.title: Creating Mutual Agreement
sessions.key_problem: Sales conversations end without a clear decision or next step because Up Front Contracts aren't being set, leaving both sides mystified about what happens next.
sessions.light_bulb: Nearly every meeting that ends in something other than yes or no is a failure to set expectations up front — bookending every conversation with a strong Up Front Contract forces real decisions instead of vague follow-ups.
sessions.scenario: Meetings keep ending in "let me think about it" because clear expectations for what a decision looks like were never set.
key_rules: No mutual mystification
If you want to know the future, bring it back to the present
The best way to get rid of a bomb is to defuse it before it explodes
You cant get mad at someone for doing something you didn't tell them they couldn't do

sessions.title: Discovering Buyer's Motivations
sessions.key_problem: Latching onto the surface-level problem a prospect states and rushing to prescribe a fix, without digging for the deeper, personal, emotional pain that actually drives a buying decision.
sessions.light_bulb: Pain has three layers -- the surface problem, the underlying reasons/root cause, and the personal or financial impact -- and buying happens on emotion first, justified with logic after, so real pain only surfaces after digging past what the prospect first says.
sessions.scenario: A prospect names a problem, the pitch jumps straight to a solution, and the real, personal pain that would have closed the deal never surfaces.
key_rules: No Pain, No Sale
You can't sell anybody anything. They must discover they want it.
People make buying decisions emotionally. They justify their decisions intellectually.
The problem the prospect brings you is never the real problem.
Prescription without diagnosis is malpractice.

links.mac_deck: /Users/danfaber/Documents/Training/Beautiful AI Decks 2026/Essentials - Sales/06. Essentials - Discovering Buyer's Motivations.pptx

sessions.title: Better Understanding Through Asking Questions
sessions.key_problem: Answering every question a prospect throws out at face value, losing control of the conversation instead of uncovering the real question or pain underneath it.
sessions.light_bulb: Most surface-level prospect questions aren't the real question, and reversing (with softening statements, done deliberately, the professional way) keeps control, uncovers truth, and lets the prospect connect their own dots.
sessions.scenario: Rapid-fire prospect questions come in and every one gets answered on instinct, handing over control of the call.
key_rules: The questions people ask you are never the real questions
No mind reading
When a customer becomes emotionally involved, they never see the reverse
Your value as a sales professional is determined more by the amount of information you gather vs the information that you give
The professional does what the novice does, but on purpose.

links.mac_deck: /Users/danfaber/Documents/Training/Beautiful AI Decks 2026/Essentials - Sales/07. Essentials - Better Understanding Through Asking Questions.pptx

sessions.title: Understanding Investment Parameters
sessions.key_problem: Avoiding or fumbling investment conversations because of personal beliefs about money, letting prospects lowball, dodge, or mislead on budget.
sessions.light_bulb: Reluctance to discuss money is usually a personal hang-up on the selling side, not the prospect's — investment conversations build trust when they're tied back to pain instead of avoided, using tactics like bracketing or "if you had to guess."
sessions.scenario: Flinching or going quiet the moment money comes up, letting prospects control the budget conversation.
key_rules: Price is never the real issue
Money does grow on trees
The prospect must be willing and able to make the necessary investment

sessions.title: Identifying the Decision Making Process
sessions.key_problem: Never mapping who is actually involved in a prospect's decision process, and complying with whatever process the buyer describes instead of guiding it.
sessions.light_bulb: You have to be a confident decision-maker yourself and interrogate the prospect's actual who/what/when/where/why/how decision process, rather than just accepting the surface answer, in order to actually help them decide.
sessions.scenario: Deals stall for weeks because who else has to sign off, and how the decision really gets made, were never nailed down.
key_rules: Only decision makers can help others to make decisions
We must know their decision process to help them make a decision, not to comply with it
If you want to get decisions faster, make decisions faster.

sessions.title: Communicating the Solution and Closing the Sale
sessions.key_problem: Presenting solutions to prospects who were never properly qualified, resulting in stalls, changed circumstances, or getting blindsided at the close.
sessions.light_bulb: A "closing problem" is almost always a qualifying problem in disguise — every presentation has to be earned by pain, and closing questions plus an Ultimate Up Front Contract keep deals from unraveling after they feel done.
sessions.scenario: Deals look closed until the prospect goes quiet or "circumstances change," because qualification, not the close itself, was the missing piece.
key_rules: There are no free presentations
The best presentation you give, the prospect will never see
Only present to pain
On your way to the bank, keep one eye over your shoulder
The best way to defuse a bomb is before it goes off.

sessions.light_bulb: An unwritten goal is just a wish, and the real grind only happens for goals that are truly your own -- so the push is to actually write down personal and professional goals instead of drifting through an agenda set elsewhere.
sessions.scenario: Grinding hard every day with no answer for what it's actually building toward beyond this month's number.
key_rules: You are either part of your own plan, or you're a part of somebody else's

sessions.title: 4 Hats of Leadership
sessions.key_problem: Conflating leadership and management, and not knowing when to use which of the 4 leadership hats (trainer, coach, mentor, supervisor) with whom.
sessions.light_bulb: Management is for behavior, process, reports, and production; leadership is for the human being -- and each of the 4 hats requires a different focus (behavior, attitude, or technique) and derives its authority differently (title vs. relationship), so wearing the wrong hat stalls development.
sessions.scenario: Defaulting to one leadership style with everyone, whether the moment calls for training a skill, coaching behavior, mentoring attitude, or supervising results.

sessions.title: Training & Coaching
sessions.key_problem: Retraining or rescuing instead of coaching, and skipping disciplined WIMs and supervision, so accountability and results quietly slip.
sessions.light_bulb: The management job isn't meeting your own needs (efficiency, comfort) by retraining or rescuing, but building critical thinking through real coaching and consistent supervision -- and a business performs exactly as it's designed to.
sessions.scenario: Re-teaching the same skill or bailing out a deal instead of running real coaching conversations and disciplined weekly one-on-one meetings.
key_rules: We improve what we track.
You can control effort, but you cannot control outcomes.
You increase your odds through effort.
Your business is performing consistently with how it was designed (design drives behavior).

sessions.title: Deflating Pipelines
sessions.key_problem: Inspecting pipelines by asking "can you close it yet?", which trains inflated or hidden deal status instead of a genuinely predictable pipeline.
sessions.light_bulb: The guitar analogy: inspecting for the finished result creates anxiety and lying, while inspecting inputs, progress, and decision quality builds the ability to actually deliver -- inspection habits trained the very inaccurate pipeline being complained about.
sessions.scenario: A pipeline looks healthy until deals mysteriously die at the end, because the only question ever asked was "is this closing?" instead of inspecting pain, decision process, and next steps all along.
key_rules: Qualify Hard. Close easy.
If you're managing results, you're attempting to manage the past. If you're managing activity, you have influence over the future.
Losers put all of their eggs in one basket.

Your value isn't in what you know — it's in how you get your people to use what they know.

key_rules: If you don’t have priorities defined in advance, you’ll create them in the moment, and you will choose whatever is easiest.

they regulate under it — and teach their teams to do the same.

sessions.key_problem: Letting deals advance on surface-level engagement signals (excitement, questions, pricing requests) instead of objective qualification evidence, which inflates and destabilizes the pipeline.

sessions.title: Coaching for Impact
sessions.key_problem: Stopping at surface-level 'pain indicators' — in selling and in coaching — instead of digging into real business impact, so nobody can tell whether a deal is genuinely qualified or just optimistic.
sessions.light_bulb: Pain indicators are not true pain: it typically takes more than three questions — moving from logical to emotional — to get from an indicator to real impact, and the asking stops way too early because it feels like too many questions.
sessions.scenario: Deals look great in pipeline review because a 'pain' can be named, but there's no real urgency or ownership behind it, and the deal stalls the second it's time to actually decide.

sessions.title: Mo' Money, Mo' Problems

sessions.scenario: Deals sail through discovery and demo and then die the second a price shows up on paper, because nobody tied the cost of the problem to the investment early enough.
key_rules: Money does grow on trees.

sessions.title: Coaching Decision Clarity

sessions.scenario: Deals that 'need time to think' keep coming up, and the reflex is asking about timelines instead of coaching to find the missing decision.
key_rules: A decision not to make a decision is still a decision.
Only decision makers can get other people to make decisions.

sessions.title: May the Force Be With You
sessions.key_problem: Coaching better responses to objections without ever diagnosing that the objection was self-created earlier in the deal, and not knowing how to handle defensive or 'difficult' behavior in coaching.

sessions.scenario: Deals keep getting lost to the exact same objections even after coaching on how to handle them, and pipeline reviews turn into arguments the moment defensiveness shows up.
key_rules: The best way to get rid of a bomb is to diffuse it before it goes off
A sales call is not a place to get your needs met
You don't learn how to win by getting a yes, you learn how to win by getting a no
0% of your selling comes from your Critical Parent. 70% comes from your Nurturing Parent. 30% comes from your Adult. Leave your Child in the car
When under attack, fall back
You can't lose something you never had.

sessions.scenario: A week of sending emails, cleaning up the CRM, and researching accounts leaves nothing in the pipeline to show for it, because none of that was actually prospecting.

sessions.scenario: A big deal closes, the foot comes off the gas for two weeks, and the following month starts behind and stressed with an empty pipeline.

You're either in charge of your own plan, or you're part of someone else's.

sessions.title: Prospecting That Converts

sessions.scenario: The same 'send me some info' or 'we're all good' brush-off comes for the tenth time this month, and there's still no prepared way to diffuse it before it happens.

Talk tracks are good, scripts are bad.

sessions.light_bulb: The reasonable-sounding stories ("I don't want to seem pushy," "I'm more about relationship selling") are actually fear-based excuses that prioritize comfort over effectiveness, and those old beliefs can be consciously reframed into new ones (e.g., "I value pain because it helps my prospect gain clarity") that support a deliberate stretch move.
sessions.scenario: The hard parts of the process keep getting skipped — the money talk, the pushy follow-up, killing the dead deal — and called personal style instead of what it really is: avoidance.
key_rules: If you don’t have priorities defined in advance, you'll create them in the moment, and you will choose whatever is easiest.

No mind-reading
Your value as a salesperson is determined more by the amount of information you gather than by the amount of information you dispense
Prospects buy for their reasons, not the salesperson's reasons.

sessions.title: From Indicator to Impact
sessions.key_problem: Mistaking the surface-level problem a prospect mentions for real pain, stopping qualification too early, and chasing deals that were never real.
sessions.light_bulb: What's been called "pain" is just an indicator; it takes several questions moving from logical to emotional impact, plus a test of ownership/urgency/willingness to act, before pain is actually proven.
sessions.scenario: A deal feels great because the prospect complained about something, then goes quiet after the demo with no clear explanation why.
key_rules: No pain, no sale.

sessions.title: Money, money, money....MONEY!
sessions.key_problem: Bringing up money either too early or too late, with personal discomfort around money shaping when and how budget gets qualified.
sessions.light_bulb: Personal money tolerance and buying habits drive the avoidance of budget talk, and pricing the size of the problem (not the product) makes money conversations feel natural and timely instead of awkward and late.
sessions.scenario: Money talk gets avoided until the formal quote, then sticker shock or a stalled deal blindsides the sale because cost was never connected to the size of the problem.
key_rules: Money does grow on trees.

sessions.title: Decisions, Decisions

sessions.light_bulb: A final yes/no is really the sum of many mini-decisions throughout the process, and stalled deals are usually breakdowns in Pain or Budget rather than buyer bad faith—so the job is to actively guide the buyer's Process, Criteria, Timeline, and Who instead of just asking "what's your timeline?"
sessions.scenario: Deals keep stalling with "let's think about it" and the prospect gets the blame, when nobody ever helped the buyer build an actual process for deciding.
key_rules: A decision not to make a decision is still a decision.
Only decision makers can get other people to make decisions.

sessions.title: The Call is Coming from Inside the House
sessions.key_problem: Treating objections as things that just happen, when most are actually self-inflicted earlier in the sale by a need for approval, emotional involvement, and fear of rejection.
sessions.light_bulb: Objections aren't random -- it's fighting a fire you started; your own DNA creates the objection, your ego state determines how it unfolds, and Equal Business Stature determines whether you stay in control of the conversation.
sessions.scenario: "We're happy with our vendor" or "need to think about it" keeps coming up and the prospect gets blamed, without seeing it was set up earlier in the call.
key_rules: The best way to get rid of a bomb is to diffuse it before it goes off.
A sales call is not a place to get your needs met.
Never get emotionally involved in the call
You don’t learn how to win by getting a yes, you learn how to win by getting a no
0% of your selling comes from your Critical Parent. 70% comes from your Nurturing Parent. 30% comes from your Adult. Leave your Child in the car.
When under attack, fall back.
You can’t lose something you never had.

The problem the prospect brings you is never the real problem.

Express your feelings through third-party stories.

sessions.title: Mastering the Negotiatior's Mindset
sessions.key_problem: Treating negotiating as a separate skill from selling and blaming the negotiation itself, when most negotiating problems are actually sales problems (weak discovery, poor preparation, no ground rules) that surface too late; six hidden weaknesses (need for approval, emotional involvement, projecting one's own buy cycle, conflict avoidance, unsupportive beliefs, rejection sensitivity) quietly sabotage leverage.
sessions.light_bulb: Buyers make decisions emotionally first and justify them with logic afterward, so appealing to logic (haggling on price/terms) misses the real lever, which is uncovering the emotional value driving the buyer's decision - and hidden weaknesses (need for approval, rejection sensitivity, etc.) are often what push toward over-explaining and giving away control.
sessions.scenario: In a price negotiation, the deal feels like it's slipping, and over-explaining or justifying the price kicks in, without realizing that talking too much is what gives away information and control.
key_rules: Most negotiating problems are selling problems.

The one who is talking is giving more information.
The person who wants it more loses control of the deal.

sessions.title: Buyer Insights Unveiled
sessions.key_problem: Getting out-maneuvered by buyer "power plays" (hiding, rushing decisions, refusing time) and unconsciously responding from a Child or Critical Parent ego state instead of staying in an Adult/Nurturing Parent posture, which hands control of the conversation to the buyer.
sessions.light_bulb: Reflexive responses to a buyer's "Critical Parent" language (like "send me a quote and I'll get back to you") often come from an Adaptive Child ego state left over from childhood conditioning, and consciously answering from Nurturing Parent or Adult - asking a question back instead of complying - keeps control of the sales process.
sessions.scenario: A prospect says "send me a quote and I'll get back to you" and the automatic response is to agree and wait, instead of recognizing the power dynamic and redirecting with a question.
key_rules: When selling, leave your child in the car (crack the window).
You are either in control of your own process, or you are part of someone else's.
Your value as a sales professional is determined more by the questions you ask than the information you give.

sessions.title: Crafting Win Win Solutions
sessions.key_problem: Going into negotiations without knowing one's own goals, levers, or minimum/target/maximum positions, so concessions (especially price) go too fast, too big, and with nothing in return.
sessions.light_bulb: Win-win negotiating (integrative, not disruptive) requires knowing both parties' real interests (not just positions), preparing goals/levers/BATNA before the conversation, and giving concessions slowly and in small pieces starting with the lowest-value item - because large, fast concessions signal your first number was fake and teach the buyer to keep asking.
sessions.scenario: A buyer pushes back on price and it drops immediately to save the deal, with no pre-planned limit on what to give up and nothing gotten back in return.
key_rules: Never make concessions unless you know the buyer's compelling reason (interests) AND their specific requests/demands and why they MUST be met.
Never concede unless you get a concession in return.
Do not accept the buyer's first attempt at getting a concession.
Articulate the value of any concession you make.
